scenes.tts: How can a machine read DNA when a polymerase handles only the next base? Watch one blue template cross the frame. A gold copy grows beside it. The machine never sees an entire chromosome. It must turn local copying events into an ordered read.

scenes.visual: Hook first. A thick blue template ribbon fills most of the frame and scrolls left while a gold copy extends beside it. A white polymerase marker rides at the growing end. Unread template continues beyond both edges. Colour map for the whole film: template blue, copied DNA gold, permanent stop red, reversible pause teal, detected signal green, uncertainty grey. Put a small 'schematic' label on every cartoon scene; use 'computed' only for a computed plot or signal.

scenes.visual: Keep the blue template and gold growing copy moving slowly in the background. Overlay only the title How Chemistry Becomes a Read for two seconds, then clear it.

scenes.tts: Sanger sequencing makes many copies from the same starting primer. Most copies take ordinary nucleotides and keep growing. Occasionally, a red dideoxynucleotide joins the copy. It lacks the usable end needed for another addition. That copy stops permanently, while other copies stop at other positions.

scenes.visual: The carried blue template fans into four parallel blue lanes, each with a gold copy starting from the same white primer block. Red stop blocks join at different positions. Each affected gold copy halts immediately while the others continue extending. Use labelled blocks, never molecular structures.

scenes.tts: The stopped copies now sort from shortest to longest. Each red endpoint carries the identity of its last base. Reading those endpoints in length order spells the newly made strand. The template runs in the opposite direction, so finding its sequence also requires reversing the complement.

scenes.visual: Transform the parallel stopped copies into a vertical length ladder occupying most of the frame. Short copies glide to the bottom and long copies to the top. Their red endpoints flash in order and feed labelled base tiles into one gold read from bottom to top. A small direction arrow flips for the blue template.

scenes.tts: Now imagine replacing the permanent red stop with a removable teal pause. What must happen before polymerase can copy the next base?
scenes.caption: Now imagine replacing the permanent red stop with a removable teal pause. What must happen before polymerase can copy the next base?
scenes.visual: Transform one red stop block into a teal pause block on the gold copy. Place a green camera icon above it and a grey question mark after it. Keep the blue template drifting under the paused copy.
scenes.narration: Now imagine replacing the permanent red stop with a removable teal pause. What must happen before polymerase can copy the next base?

scenes.visual: Hold the question on screen. The teal pause block pulses slowly, the green camera aperture moves, and the grey question mark breathes. Do not reveal the answer.

scenes.tts: The machine images the colour while every copy in a cluster is paused. Then it removes both the dye and the block. The free end can accept another nucleotide. Repeating this add, image, and reset cycle reports one new base from every cluster each time.
scenes.caption: The machine images the colour while every copy in a cluster is paused. Then it removes both the dye and the block. The free end can accept another nucleotide. Repeating this add, image, and reset cycle reports one new base from every cluster each time.
scenes.visual: Duplicate the carried gold copy into one large cluster of aligned gold strands. Teal pause blocks appear together, a green camera sweep records them, then the teal blocks lift away. All strands extend together and repeat the moving cycle. A three-state ring labelled add, image, reset rotates beside the cluster.
scenes.narration: The machine images the colour while every copy in a cluster is paused. Then it removes both the dye and the block. The free end can accept another nucleotide. Repeating this add, image, and reset cycle reports one new base from every cluster each time.

scenes.tts: This is not Sanger sequencing performed in parallel. Sanger reads a permanent ladder of fragment lengths. Short-read sequencing follows temporary pauses through repeated cycles. Millions of clusters can work together, and both ends of each fragment can be read. Yet each reported stretch remains short.

scenes.visual: Split the frame without changing colours. On the left, the red-ended Sanger ladder sorts once. On the right, teal pauses cycle across a field of gold clusters. The field zooms outward to imply many clusters, then a single short fragment is read inward from both ends. Label the diagrams schematic.

scenes.tts: Long-read methods follow single molecules instead. In one method, a polymerase circles the same template repeatedly, letting repeated passes support a consensus. In the other, a strand moves through a pore while changing ionic current. Software converts that moving signal into bases. Both approaches preserve longer-range context.

scenes.visual: Transform the short gold fragment into one long gold ribbon. First it loops past the white polymerase marker several times while green base calls stack into consensus tiles. Then the same ribbon straightens and threads through a labelled pore block. A green current trace marked schematic turns into base tiles. No molecular structures.

scenes.tts: These methods do not merely differ in speed. The chemistry, the DNA fragments loaded, and base-calling software together shape read length, error pattern, and context. A read is still evidence from one fragment, not a chromosome. Later analysis must decide where it belongs. Genome results depend on what each read records and where it fits.

scenes.visual: Bring back the full blue template. Red-ended ladder fragments, short gold cluster reads, and one long gold read transform into three labelled evidence cards. Each card slides toward several possible positions on the blue ribbon. Grey question marks remain over the placements; do not resolve them yet.

scenes.tts: Sequencing turns molecular events into ordered base calls. A polymerase stop, a cycle of coloured pauses, or a changing current becomes an ordered string. The chemistry shapes what evidence reaches the computer. That distinction will guide every calculation and genome comparison that follows. The next question is whether those strings fit one genomic path or several.
